issue.issue_text: Whether a pre-constitutional law, which became inoperative under Article 13(1) for being inconsistent with a fundamental right, can be revived and become operative again after a constitutional amendment removes that inconsistency.

facts: The case involved a pre-constitutional law, the C.P. & Berar Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act, 1947, which allowed the government to create a monopoly in the motor transport business.
When the Indian Constitution came into force in 1950, this law became inconsistent with the fundamental right to practice a profession under Article 19(1)(g).

Subsequently, the Constitution was amended (First and Fourth Amendments), which altered the fundamental rights provisions (specifically Articles 19(6) and 31) in a way that removed the inconsistency and permitted state monopolies.
The petitioners argued that the law, having become 'void' under Article 13(1), was dead and could not be revived by a constitutional amendment unless it was re-enacted by the legislature.
law: The Court interpreted the word 'void' in Article 13(1), which states that pre-constitutional laws inconsistent with fundamental rights are 'void to the extent of such inconsistency'.

It held that 'void' does not mean the law is completely wiped out or dead for all purposes. The law is only rendered inoperative or unenforceable against those who possess the fundamental right (i.e., citizens).
The Court explained this using the 'doctrine of eclipse'. The fundamental right 'overshadows' or 'eclipses' the inconsistent law, making it dormant but not nullifying it entirely.
The law remains valid for past transactions (pre-Constitution) and continues to apply to non-citizens who are not granted the specific fundamental right.
application: The Court applied the doctrine of eclipse to the situation. The pre-constitutional law was not dead but was merely eclipsed by the fundamental right under Article 19(1)(g) as it originally stood.
The subsequent constitutional amendments had the effect of 'removing the shadow' or the eclipse that was cast by the fundamental right.

Since the law was never dead, but only dormant, the removal of the constitutional inconsistency automatically revived the law and made it fully operative and enforceable again from the date of the amendment.
The Court clarified that this revival was not retrospective. The law remained inoperative for the period between the commencement of the Constitution and the date of the constitutional amendment.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that a pre-constitutional law, which becomes inoperative ('eclipsed') under Article 13(1) for being inconsistent with a fundamental right, is not permanently dead. It can be revived and become fully operative again if a subsequent constitutional amendment removes the inconsistency, without requiring the legislature to re-enact the law.

issue.issue_text: Whether the precedents set in Shagir Ahmad v. The State of U.P. & Others and Behrom Khurshed Pesikaka v. The State of Bombay were applicable to the present case.

facts: The petitioners challenged a 1947 Act, arguing that it became void when the Constitution came into force in 1950 because it was inconsistent with fundamental rights.
To support their argument, the petitioners relied on the precedent set in the case of *Shagir Ahmad v. The State of U.P. & Others*.
law: The Court considered a legal argument that was not raised in the *Shagir Ahmad* case.
This argument was that a pre-constitutional law that is inconsistent with a fundamental right is not completely dead, but merely dormant or "overshadowed."
If a subsequent constitutional amendment removes the inconsistency, the dormant law is revived and becomes operative again.
application: The Supreme Court noted that the specific question of whether a constitutional amendment could revive a dormant law was never raised or considered in the *Shagir Ahmad* case.

The text explicitly states, "This question was not considered by this Court in Shagir Ahmad's case, for it was there conceded... that the validity of the U. P. Act..." was inconsistent with the Constitution.
Since the central legal issue of the present case was not addressed in the prior case, the precedent was not controlling.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the applicability of the precedents, distinguishing them on the grounds that the core legal question in the present case—the revival of a dormant law by a constitutional amendment—had not been raised or decided in those earlier cases.

issue.issue_text: Whether the petitioners could challenge the validity of the impugned Act on the ground that it infringed their fundamental rights under Article 31(2), in view of the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act of 1955.

facts.fact: The Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1955, which amended Article 31, came into force on April 27, 1955.
The petitioners filed their writ petitions on May 27, 1955, exactly one month after the amendment took effect.

law.description: A pre-constitutional law that is inconsistent with a fundamental right is not permanently void or dead, but is merely overshadowed or rendered dormant. If a subsequent constitutional amendment removes the inconsistency, the law is revivified and becomes fully operative from the date of the amendment.

application.step: The Court acknowledged that the impugned Act was inconsistent with the original Article 31(2) when the Constitution came into force and remained so until the Fourth Amendment.

However, the Court determined that the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1955, removed this inconsistency. Under the amended Article 31, the impugned Act was no longer unconstitutional as it did not provide for the transfer of ownership or right to possession of any property.
Applying the same reasoning it used for the First Amendment (the doctrine of eclipse), the Court found that the impugned Act was revived and became fully operative from April 27, 1955.
Since the petitioners filed their case after the amendment had come into force, the law they were challenging was constitutionally valid at the time of their petition.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the petitioners' challenge. It held that because the petitions were filed after the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1955, had removed the inconsistency between the impugned Act and Article 31(2), the petitioners could not be permitted to challenge the Act's validity on that ground.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in considering the sentence imposed by the Sessions Judge as manifestly inadequate and enhancing it.

facts: The Sessions Judge imposed a sentence on the accused.
The High Court later enhanced this sentence, on the grounds that it was 'manifestly inadequate'.
law: For a High Court to be justified in enhancing a sentence imposed by a lower court, it must provide adequate reasons for why the original sentence is considered 'manifestly inadequate'.
application: The Supreme Court examined the circumstances of the case and determined that the sentence imposed by the Sessions Judge was, in fact, a 'substantial sentence'.
The Court found that the High Court had failed to provide any 'adequate reason' to support its conclusion that the Sessions Judge's sentence was 'manifestly inadequate'.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was not justified in enhancing the sentence. Therefore, the appeal was allowed, the High Court's enhanced sentence was set aside, and the original sentence from the Sessions Court was restored.

cases.principle: A law that is void under Article 13(1) for being inconsistent with the Constitution still existed for all past transactions and for the enforcement of rights and liabilities that accrued before the date the Constitution came into force.

cases.case_name: Shagir Ahmad v. The State of U.P. & Others
cases.principle: A law that sanctioned a total prohibition on the right to carry on an innocuous business (like motor transport) could not be justified as a 'reasonable restriction' under the original version of Article 19(6) of the Constitution.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A pre-constitutional law that is inconsistent with a fundamental right is not rendered void from its inception but is merely eclipsed by the fundamental right. Such a law remains valid for pre-constitutional transactions and for non-citizens. If a subsequent constitutional amendment removes the inconsistency, the eclipse is lifted, and the law becomes fully operative again without the need for re-enactment.
obiter: American legal authorities, which hold that post-constitutional laws inconsistent with a constitution are 'still born' and void from inception, do not apply to pre-constitutional laws in India which were valid before the Constitution came into force.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A pre-constitutional law that becomes inconsistent with a fundamental right upon the commencement of the Constitution is not rendered permanently void or dead. Instead, under Article 13(1), such a law is merely 'eclipsed' by the fundamental right, remaining dormant and inoperative against citizens for the duration of the inconsistency. If a subsequent constitutional amendment removes the conflict, the eclipse is lifted, and the pre-constitutional law is automatically revivified and becomes fully operative and enforceable without the need for re-enactment.
legal_tests_applied: Doctrine of Eclipse: This doctrine distinguishes between pre-constitutional laws and post-constitutional laws. Pre-constitutional laws, valid at their inception, are not nullified by the Constitution but are merely rendered ineffectual or overshadowed to the extent of their inconsistency with fundamental rights. Post-constitutional laws inconsistent with fundamental rights are considered void ab initio or 'still born'.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's contention that the impugned Act, having become void for unconstitutionality, was dead and could not be vitalised by a subsequent constitutional amendment was rejected. The court held that the law was not dead but merely eclipsed, and the amendment removed the eclipse.

The appellant's reliance on the precedent in Shagir Ahmad's case was misplaced, as the court held it had no application to the present facts, which involved the effect of a constitutional amendment on a pre-constitutional law.
The appellant's challenge based on Article 31(2) was rejected. (The provided text does not contain the court's reasoning for this specific rejection).
The appellant's argument regarding the enhancement of the sentence was accepted, not lost.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's argument that the impugned Act was merely eclipsed by the fundamental right and not rendered permanently void was accepted as 'well-founded'.
The court reasoned that the effect of the Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951 was 'to remove the shadow and to make the impugned Act free from all blemish or infirmity,' thus reviving it.

The court supported this reasoning by noting that such eclipsed laws were not dead for all purposes; they continued to exist for pre-Constitution rights and liabilities and remained operative against non-citizens, proving they were merely in a 'dormant or moribund condition' with respect to citizens' fundamental rights.

The court distinguished American authorities on unconstitutionality, stating they apply to post-Constitution laws which are 'still born,' whereas pre-Constitution laws were perfectly valid before the Constitution and thus could be revived.
policy_considerations: The court's reasoning gives effect to the intent of constitutional amendments designed to save existing laws. The court noted that if eclipsed laws were considered permanently void, it would be unintelligible what 'existing law' the Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951 could have sought to save, as all such laws would have already been voided.
